messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Translating a JAGS module for Stan?
parts:
Hi folks,

For decades it has been known that human response data from experiments involving simple perceptual discriminations are very well fit by a "diffusion model" consisting of a Wiener process unfolding through time between two bounds (reaching a bound causes the process to terminate, determining a response and the response time). I'd like to use Stan to perform inference on a hierarchical version of such a model (aggregating data from multiple human subjects, each measured hundreds of times). Apparently there already exists code in the form of a JAGS module (http://sourceforge.net/projects/jags-wiener/) that implements the sort of model I'd like to implement. Any advice on how I should go about translating this for use with Stan? Or are there tools already in Stan that could be used to implement this sort of model?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

you could always just model both y and t and then forget
about y. Basically, MCMC would do the integration for you.

or Fortran iterative code to templated C++. The derivatives would
be slow if many iterations are required. If there were
a way to compute the derivatives directly (even if iterative),
that would be much faster.

3. Next year, we'll be working on building in diff eq solvers
for implicit equations, but I'm not sure that'll help here.

- Bob

parts:
I've also been puzzled by trying to implement this model in Stan. If it helps the discussion along, I have some R code to simulate and illustrate this kind of model:

https://gist.github.com/crowding/5846850

That Tuerlinckx paper is pretty heady. Here's a simpler introduction to the topic: http://www.shadlenlab.columbia.edu/~mike/papers/mine/okinawa_chapter2006.pdf

For most of the questions the mathematical psychologists have about such models (e.g. are bounds time-varying, is a single decision variable enough, how to deal with N>2 choices), finding closed form solutions for the likelihood function is a fool's errand. In practice, what people do is discretize the response time and the decision variable(s) over a grid, for each distinct type of trial, and then numerically sum out the Fokker-Planck equation from there to get likelihoods.

That's also the best idea I have for implementing this model in Stan, but I'm not sure if the gradient calculations can cope with it.

(Other possibilities are making the noise an explicit vector parameter for each trial, which would lead to an explosion of parameters.)

Peter Meilstrup
Physiology and Biophysics
University of Washington

Joachim
